Groups have one operation. Most of the algebra you already use has two: integers, polynomials and matrices can be added and multiplied, and the distributive law ties the two together. A structure with both is a ring. This post builds ring theory the same way posts 01–03 built group theory: definitions and examples, then substructures (ideals play the role of normal subgroups), quotients and a First Isomorphism Theorem. Two questions then drive the rest. Which rings behave like Z, with unique factorisation? And how do you manufacture new fields, such as C or a field with 4 elements? The answer to the second, "take polynomials modulo an irreducible polynomial", is the starting point of Galois theory in post 05.
Series map: 00 Integers, Relations & Modular Arithmetic → 01 Groups & Subgroups → 02 Cosets, Lagrange & Quotient Groups → 03 Homomorphisms, Group Actions & Sylow → 04 Rings, Ideals & Fields (this post) → 05 Field Extensions & Galois Theory.

State the ring axioms (with identity), and recognise units, zero divisors, integral domains and fields.
Prove that a finite integral domain is a field and that the characteristic of a domain is 0 or a prime.
Define ring homomorphisms, ideals and quotient rings, and prove the First Isomorphism Theorem for rings.
Prove that R/P is a domain exactly when P is prime, and R/M is a field exactly when M is maximal.
Use the division algorithm in F[x] and prove that F[x] is a principal ideal domain.
Test polynomials for irreducibility: roots, the rational root test, Eisenstein's criterion, reduction mod p.
Place a ring in the chain Euclidean domain ⊂ PID ⊂ UFD ⊂ integral domain, and show that Z[−5] is not a UFD.
Build C as R[x]/(x2+1) and the finite fields F4 and F8, and compute in them.

Ring — a set R with two operations + and ⋅ such that:
(R,+) is an abelian group, with identity 0 and inverses −a;
multiplication is associative: (ab)c=a(bc);
there is a multiplicative identity 1 with 1a=a1=a;
the distributive laws hold: a(b+c)=ab+ac and (a+b)c=ac+bc.
Convention. In this series every ring has a 1 (some books call these "rings with unity" and allow rings without one). Multiplication need not be commutative.
Commutative ring — a ring with ab=ba for all a,b.
Zero ring — {0} with 1=0. It is the only ring in which 1=0 (if 1=0 then a=1a=0a=0).
Unit — an element u with a two-sided inverse: uv=vu=1. The units form a group R× under multiplication.
Zero divisor — a nonzero a for which some nonzero b has ab=0 or ba=0.
Integral domain — a commutative ring with 1≠0 and no zero divisors.
Field — a commutative ring with 1≠0 in which every nonzero element is a unit.
Division ring — like a field but not necessarily commutative (the quaternions are the standard example).

Ring · Commutative? · Units · Zero divisors?
Z · yes · ±1 · none (domain)
Q,R,C · yes · all nonzero · none (fields)
Z/nZ · yes · classes with gcd⁡(a,n)=1 · yes, unless n is prime
M2(R), 2×2 real matrices · no · matrices with det⁡≠0 · yes
R[x], real polynomials · yes · nonzero constants · none
Z[i]={a+bi:a,b∈Z} · yes · ±1,±i · none
C[0,1], continuous functions, pointwise operations · yes · functions with no zero · yes
A few of the entries, worked out:
Z/12Z. The units are 1,5,7,11 (coprime to 12; each is its own inverse, e.g. 5⋅5=25≡1). Every other nonzero class is a zero divisor: 2⋅6=12≡0, 3⋅4≡0, 8⋅3≡0, and so on, giving 2,3,4,6,8,9,10. In Z/nZ every nonzero element is either a unit or a zero divisor: if d=gcd⁡(a,n)>1, then a⋅(n/d)≡0 with n/d≢0.
Matrices. (1000)(0001)=(0000), although neither factor is zero.
Gaussian integers. Use the norm N(a+bi)=a2+b2=(a+bi)(a−bi), which is multiplicative: N(zw)=N(z)N(w). If uv=1 then N(u)N(v)=1 in the positive integers, so N(u)=1, and a2+b2=1 leaves ±1,±i.
Functions. Let f be zero on [0,12] and g zero on [12,1], both continuous and not identically zero (for example f(t)=max⁡(0,t−12), g(t)=max⁡(0,12−t)). Then fg=0.

For all a,b in a ring:
0⋅a=a⋅0=0. Proof: 0a=(0+0)a=0a+0a; subtract 0a from both sides.
(−a)b=a(−b)=−(ab). Proof: ab+(−a)b=(a+(−a))b=0b=0.
(−a)(−b)=ab, and in particular (−1)2=1.
Cancellation. In an integral domain, if a≠0 and ab=ac then b=c, because a(b−c)=0 forces b−c=0. This is exactly what fails in Z/12Z: 2⋅1=2⋅7 but 1≠7.
Every field is an integral domain: if a≠0 and ab=0, then b=a−1ab=0. The converse fails (Z), except for finite rings:
Theorem. A finite integral domain is a field.
Proof. Let R be a finite domain and a≠0. The map μa:R→R, x↦ax, is injective by cancellation. An injective map from a finite set to itself is surjective, so ax=1 for some x. Since R is commutative, x is a two-sided inverse. ∎
Corollary. Z/nZ is a field if and only if n is prime. (If n=ab with 1<a,b<n, then a and b are zero divisors. If n=p is prime, Z/pZ has no zero divisors because p∣ab implies p∣a or p∣b, post 00; so it is a finite domain.) This field is written Fp.

The characteristic of a ring R is the least n≥1 with n⋅1=1+1+⋯+1=0 (n terms), or 0 if there is no such n. So char⁡Z=char⁡Q=0 and char⁡Z/nZ=n.
Theorem. The characteristic of an integral domain is 0 or a prime.
Proof. Suppose char⁡R=n>0 and n=ab with 1≤a,b<n. Then 0=n⋅1=(a⋅1)(b⋅1). In a domain one factor is 0, contradicting the minimality of n. And n≠1 because 1≠0. ∎
Watch out: characteristic is about n⋅1, not about the size of the ring. The infinite field Fp(t) of rational functions over Fp has characteristic p.

Subring — a subset S⊆R containing 1 that is closed under +, − and ⋅. Example: Z⊂Z[i]⊂C.
Ring homomorphism — a map φ:R→S with φ(a+b)=φ(a)+φ(b), φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b) and φ(1)=1.
Kernel — ker⁡φ={a:φ(a)=0}.
Ideal — an additive subgroup I⊆R that absorbs multiplication: ra∈I and ar∈I for all r∈R, a∈I. (For commutative rings one condition suffices.)
Principal ideal — in a commutative ring, (a)=aR={ra:r∈R}, the smallest ideal containing a. More generally (a1,…,ak)={r1a1+⋯+rkak}.
Examples of homomorphisms: reduction Z→Z/nZ; evaluation R[x]→C, f↦f(i); complex conjugation C→C; the inclusion of a subring.

Theorem. The kernel of a ring homomorphism is an ideal.
Proof. It is an additive subgroup, being the kernel of a homomorphism of additive groups (post 03). If φ(a)=0 then φ(ra)=φ(r)⋅0=0 and φ(ar)=0. ∎
Ideals are to rings what normal subgroups are to groups: exactly the things you can take a quotient by. Two quick facts:
If an ideal I contains a unit u, then I=R: for any r, r=(ru−1)u∈I. So a proper ideal contains no units, and in particular does not contain 1.
A commutative ring R with 1≠0 is a field if and only if its only ideals are {0} and R. (If R is a field, any nonzero ideal contains a unit. Conversely, for a≠0, (a)=R∋1, so ra=1 for some r.) Consequently every ring homomorphism from a field to a nonzero ring is injective: its kernel is a proper ideal (it misses 1), hence {0}.
Theorem. Every ideal of Z is nZ=(n) for a unique n≥0.
Proof. Let I≠{0} and let n be the least positive element of I. For a∈I divide: a=qn+r with 0≤r<n. Then r=a−qn∈I, so r=0 by minimality, and a∈(n). ∎
In Z, (a,b)=(gcd⁡(a,b)): for example (4,6)=(2). This is Bézout's identity from post 00 in ideal language.

Let I be an ideal of R. The additive cosets a+I form an abelian group R/I (post 02). Define multiplication by (a+I)(b+I)=ab+I.
Well defined. If a′=a+i and b′=b+j with i,j∈I, then a′b′=ab+(aj+ib+ij), and the bracket lies in I because I absorbs multiplication. This is precisely where "ideal" (rather than just "subring") is needed. The ring axioms for R/I follow from those of R, with 1+I as identity, and π:R→R/I, a↦a+I, is a surjective homomorphism with kernel I.
Theorem (First Isomorphism Theorem for rings). If φ:R→S is a ring homomorphism, then R/ker⁡φ≅im⁡φ via a+ker⁡φ↦φ(a).
Proof. By the group version (post 03) the map φˉ is a well-defined isomorphism of additive groups. It is multiplicative: φˉ((a+K)(b+K))=φˉ(ab+K)=φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b); and φˉ(1+K)=φ(1)=1. ∎
Worked applications:
Z[x]/(x)≅Z. Evaluation at 0, f↦f(0), is surjective, and its kernel is the polynomials with zero constant term, which is (x).
R[x]/(x2+1)≅C. Evaluation at i is surjective (a+bx↦a+bi). Its kernel contains x2+1; Chapter 6 shows that (x2+1) is a maximal ideal, so the kernel (a proper ideal containing it) is exactly (x2+1).
Z[x]/(2,x)≅Z/2Z. The map f↦f(0) mod 2 is surjective with kernel {f:f(0) even}=(2,x).
Chinese Remainder Theorem. If gcd⁡(m,n)=1, the map Z→Z/m×Z/n, a↦(a mod m,a mod n), is a surjective ring homomorphism (surjective by post 00's CRT) with kernel (m)∩(n)=(mn). So Z/mnZ≅Z/mZ×Z/nZ as rings, and taking units gives ϕ(mn)=ϕ(m)ϕ(n) for Euler's function.
Trick: the fastest way to understand R/I is again to find a surjective homomorphism out of R whose kernel is I. Evaluation maps are the usual candidates for polynomial rings.

Prime ideal — a proper ideal P such that ab∈P implies a∈P or b∈P.
Maximal ideal — a proper ideal M such that no ideal lies strictly between M and R: if M⊆J⊆R then J=M or J=R.
In Z: (p) for a prime p is prime (this is Euclid's lemma) and maximal; (0) is prime (because Z is a domain) but not maximal, since (0)⊊(2)⊊Z; (6) is neither, since 2⋅3∈(6) but 2,3∉(6).

Theorem. P is a prime ideal of R if and only if R/P is an integral domain.
Proof. R/P is not the zero ring exactly when 1∉P, i.e. when P is proper. In R/P, the product (a+P)(b+P)=ab+P is zero exactly when ab∈P, and a+P is zero exactly when a∈P. So "no zero divisors in R/P" says word for word "ab∈P⇒a∈P or b∈P". ∎
Theorem. M is a maximal ideal of R if and only if R/M is a field.
Proof. (⇒) Let a+M≠0, i.e. a∉M. The ideal M+(a)={m+ra} strictly contains M, so by maximality it is R and contains 1: 1=m+ra for some m∈M, r∈R. Then (r+M)(a+M)=ra+M=1−m+M=1+M, so a+M is a unit. Also 1+M≠0 because M is proper.
(⇐) If R/M is a field, M is proper. Let M⊊J and pick a∈J∖M. Then a+M has an inverse r+M, so ra−1∈M⊆J. Since ra∈J, also 1∈J and J=R. ∎
Corollary. Every maximal ideal is prime (a field is a domain).
Examples in Z[x].
(x) is prime but not maximal: Z[x]/(x)≅Z is a domain but not a field. Indeed (x)⊊(2,x)⊊Z[x].
(2,x) is maximal: Z[x]/(2,x)≅Z/2Z, a field.
(x2+1) is prime but not maximal: Z[x]/(x2+1)≅Z[i], a domain that is not a field.
A standard existence result (it needs Zorn's lemma): every proper ideal of a ring with 1 is contained in a maximal ideal.

Let F be a field. F[x] is the ring of polynomials a0+a1x+⋯+anxn with ai∈F. If an≠0, the degree is n and an is the leading coefficient; the polynomial is monic if an=1. The zero polynomial has no degree (some books use −∞).

If R is a domain, the leading coefficient of fg is the product of the leading coefficients, which is nonzero. Hence, for nonzero f,g:
deg⁡(fg)=deg⁡f+deg⁡g,
R[x] is again a domain, and the units of F[x] are the nonzero constants (a unit f has deg⁡f+deg⁡f−1=0).
Theorem (division algorithm). For f,g∈F[x] with g≠0 there are unique q,r∈F[x] with f=qg+r and either r=0 or deg⁡r<deg⁡g.
Proof sketch. Existence by induction on deg⁡f: if deg⁡f≥deg⁡g=m, subtract (an/bm) xn−mg to kill the leading term of f and apply induction to the result. Dividing by bm is where a field is used. Uniqueness: if qg+r=q′g+r′ then (q−q′)g=r′−r; the right side has degree <m, so q=q′ by the degree formula, and then r=r′. ∎
Worked example. Divide f=x4+3x3−2x+5 by g=x2+x+1 in Q[x]:
x4+3x3−2x+5=(x2+x+1)(x2+2x−3)+(8−x).
(Check: (x2+x+1)(x2+2x−3)=x4+3x3−x−3, and adding 8−x gives f.)
Factor theorem. a is a root of f if and only if (x−a)∣f (divide by x−a; the remainder is the constant f(a)). So a nonzero polynomial of degree n over a domain has at most n roots.
Common pitfall: over a ring with zero divisors this fails. In Z/8Z, x2−1 has four roots: 1,3,5,7 (each squares to 1 mod 8).

A principal ideal domain (PID) is an integral domain in which every ideal is principal.
Theorem. If F is a field, F[x] is a PID.
Proof. Let I≠{0} be an ideal and let g∈I be nonzero of least degree. For f∈I write f=qg+r. Then r=f−qg∈I and, if r≠0, deg⁡r<deg⁡g, contradicting minimality. So r=0 and I=(g). ∎
The proof is the one for Z with "size" replaced by "degree". As in Z, (f,g)=(gcd⁡(f,g)), and the Euclidean algorithm computes the gcd:
x6−1=x2 (x4−1)+(x2−1),x4−1=(x2+1)(x2−1)+0,
so gcd⁡(x6−1,x4−1)=x2−1.
Watch out: Z[x] is not a PID, although Z is. Suppose (2,x)=(h). Then h∣2, so h is a constant ±1 or ±2. h=±1 is impossible because (2,x) is proper (its quotient is Z/2). h=±2 is impossible because x∉(2).

A nonzero non-unit f∈F[x] is irreducible if it is not a product of two polynomials of smaller degree. Irreducible polynomials are the "primes" of F[x], and whether f is irreducible depends on the field: x2−2 is irreducible over Q but factors as (x−2)(x+2) over R; x2+1 is irreducible over R but not over C.
Degree 2 or 3. A polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over a field is irreducible if and only if it has no root in the field (any factorisation includes a linear factor).
Rational root test. If f=anxn+⋯+a0∈Z[x] and p/q in lowest terms is a root, then p∣a0 and q∣an.
Gauss's lemma. A polynomial in Z[x] that factors in Q[x] into factors of lower degree already factors in Z[x] into factors of those same degrees. So it suffices to look for integer factorisations.
Eisenstein's criterion. Let f=anxn+⋯+a0∈Z[x] and p a prime with p∤an, p∣ai for all i<n, and p2∤a0. Then f is irreducible in Q[x].
Reduction mod p. Let f∈Z[x] and let p be a prime not dividing the leading coefficient. If the reduction fˉ∈Fp[x] is irreducible (of the same degree), then f is irreducible in Q[x].
Worked examples:
x3−2: Eisenstein with p=2. Also, the rational root test leaves only ±1,±2, none of which is a root.
x3+2x+1: candidates ±1 give 4 and −2, so no rational root; degree 3, so irreducible over Q.
x5−4x+2: Eisenstein with p=2 (2∣−4, 2∣2, 4∤2). This polynomial returns in post 05.
Cyclotomic polynomial

test leaves only ±1,±2, none of which is a root.
x3+2x+1: candidates ±1 give 4 and −2, so no rational root; degree 3, so irreducible over Q.
x5−4x+2: Eisenstein with p=2 (2∣−4, 2∣2, 4∤2). This polynomial returns in post 05.
Cyclotomic polynomial Φ5(x)=x4+x3+x2+x+1=(x5−1)/(x−1). Eisenstein does not apply directly, but f(x) is irreducible exactly when f(x+1) is, and
Φ5(x+1)=x4+5x3+10x2+10x+5, which is Eisenstein at 5.
x4+5x3+3x2+7x+11: reduce mod 2 to x4+x3+x2+x+1, which is irreducible in F2[x]. So the original is irreducible over Q.
Common pitfall: "no rational roots" proves irreducibility only in degree 2 and 3. x4+4 has no rational root, yet x4+4=(x2+2x+2)(x2−2x+2).
Common pitfall: the reduction test only works one way. x2+1 is irreducible over Q, but mod 2 it is (x+1)2. A reducible reduction proves nothing; so does a failed Eisenstein check.

In an integral domain R:
a divides b, written a∣b, if b=ac for some c∈R.
a and b are associates if a=ub for a unit u (for example 2 and −2 in Z, or 1+i and i(1+i)=−1+i in Z[i]).
A nonzero non-unit p is irreducible if p=ab forces a or b to be a unit.
A nonzero non-unit p is prime if p∣ab forces p∣a or p∣b (equivalently, (p) is a prime ideal).
Unique factorisation domain (UFD) — a domain in which every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducibles, uniquely up to order and associates.
Euclidean domain — a domain with a function N:R∖{0}→Z≥0 such that for all a and b≠0 there are q,r with a=qb+r and r=0 or N(r)<N(b).
Prime implies irreducible in any domain: if p is prime and p=ab, then p∣ab, say p∣a, so a=pc and p=pcb; cancelling gives cb=1, so b is a unit. The converse holds in a UFD (and so in a PID) but fails in general, which is exactly how unique factorisation breaks.

fields⊂Euclidean domains⊂PIDs⊂UFDs⊂integral domains.
Euclidean ⇒ PID: the proof that F[x] is a PID works verbatim with N in place of degree.
PID ⇒ UFD: a standard theorem (existence uses the fact that increasing chains of ideals in a PID stop; uniqueness uses "irreducible ⇒ prime" in a PID).
Every inclusion is strict, as the diagram's examples show.

Take N(a+bi)=a2+b2. To divide α by β, compute α/β in C and round each coordinate to the nearest integer to get q; the rounding error has both coordinates at most 12, so N(α/β−q)≤14+14<1 and r=α−qβ has N(r)<N(β).
Worked example. Divide 7+2i by 2−i:
7+2i2−i=(7+2i)(2+i)5=12+11i5=2.4+2.2i.
Round to q=2+2i. Then r=(7+2i)−(2+2i)(2−i)=(7+2i)−(6+2i)=1, and N(1)=1<N(2−i)=5. So Z[i] is a PID and a UFD.

Let R=Z[−5]={a+b−5:a,b∈Z} with norm N(a+b−5)=a2+5b2, again multiplicative. In R,
6=2⋅3=(1+−5)(1−−5).
Norms. N(2)=4, N(3)=9, N(1±−5)=1+5=6.
Units. N(u)=1 forces a2+5b2=1, so u=±1.
All four factors are irreducible. A proper factor of an element of norm 4, 9 or 6 would have norm 2 or 3. But a2+5b2=2 or 3 has no integer solutions (b≠0 gives at least 5; b=0 needs a2∈{2,3}).
The factorisations really differ. 2 is not an associate of 1±−5 (the only units are ±1, and the norms 4 and 6 differ).
So R is not a UFD. Equivalently, 2 is irreducible but not prime: 2∣(1+−5)(1−−5), but 2 divides neither factor, since (1±−5)/2∉R.
The other separating examples, stated without proof: Z[x] and F[x,y] are UFDs (Gauss: R a UFD implies R[x] a UFD) but not PIDs, as shown for (2,x) above; and Z[1+−192] is a PID that is not Euclidean (Dummit & Foote, §8.1–8.2).

Theorem. Let F be a field and p∈F[x] nonconstant. Then F[x]/(p) is a field if and only if p is irreducible.
Proof. In a PID, (p) is maximal exactly when p is irreducible. If p is irreducible and (p)⊆(h), then h∣p, so h is a unit (and (h) is everything) or an associate of p (and (h)=(p)). If p=ab with a,b of lower degree, then (p)⊊(a)⊊F[x]. Now apply "maximal ⇔ quotient is a field" from Chapter 3. ∎
What the elements look like. By the division algorithm every class has exactly one representative of degree <n=deg⁡p. So F[x]/(p) is an n-dimensional vector space over F with basis 1,α,…,αn−1, where α=x+(p) is a root of p. If F=Fq is finite, the field has qn elements. To multiply, multiply polynomials and reduce with p(α)=0; to invert, use the extended Euclidean algorithm (since gcd⁡(f,p)=1, there are s,t with sf+tp=1, so s=f−1).

x2+1 has no real root, so it is irreducible over R and R[x]/(x2+1) is a field whose elements are a+bα with α2=−1:
(a+bα)(c+dα)=ac+(ad+bc)α+bd α2=(ac−bd)+(ad+bc)α.
That is exactly complex multiplication, and the evaluation map of Chapter 2 is the isomorphism with C. Example: (3+2α)(1−α)=3−3α+2α−2α2=5−α, matching (3+2i)(1−i)=5−i.

Over F2, x2+x+1 has no root (0↦1, 1↦1), so it is irreducible and F4=F2[x]/(x2+x+1) is a field with elements 0,1,α,α+1 and the rule α2=α+1 (since −1=1 in characteristic 2).
Addition (coefficients add mod 2):
+ · 0 · 1 · α · α+1
0 · 0 · 1 · α · α+1
1 · 1 · 0 · α+1 · α
α · α · α+1 · 0 · 1
α+1 · α+1 · α · 1 · 0
Multiplication:
× · 0 · 1 · α · α+1
0 · 0 · 0 · 0 · 0
1 · 0 · 1 · α · α+1
α · 0 · α · α+1 · 1
α+1 · 0 · α+1 · 1 · α
Two entries in detail: α(α+1)=α2+α=(α+1)+α=1, and (α+1)2=α2+2α+1=α2+1=α. Every nonzero element has an inverse, and the multiplicative group {1,α,α+1} is cyclic of order 3.
Common pitfall: F4 is not Z/4Z. In Z/4Z, 2⋅2=0, so it is not even a domain. The additive group of F4 is Z/2×Z/2, not Z/4.

x3+x+1 has no root in F2 (0↦1, 1↦1), so, being cubic, it is irreducible, and F8=F2[x]/(x3+x+1) has 23=8 elements c0+c1α+c2α2 with α3=α+1. The powers of α run through all 7 nonzero elements:
k · 0 · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6
αk · 1 · α · α2 · α+1 · α2+α · α2+α+1 · α2+1
and α7=α⋅α6=α3+α=1. This "log table" makes multiplication easy: αi⋅αj=α(i+j) mod 7. For example (1+α)−1=(α3)−1=α4=α2+α; check: (1+α)(α2+α)=α3+α=1.
Post 05 proves that for every prime power pn there is exactly one field of that size, up to isomorphism.

1. List the units and the zero divisors of Z/15Z.
Solution
Units are the classes coprime to 15: 1,2,4,7,8,11,13,14 (there are ϕ(15)=8). The other nonzero classes, 3,5,6,9,10,12, are zero divisors: for example 3⋅5=15≡0 and 6⋅5=30≡0.
2. Show that (x) is a prime ideal of Q[x] that is also maximal, while in Z[x] it is prime but not maximal. What changes?
Solution
Evaluation at 0 gives Q[x]/(x)≅Q, a field, so (x) is maximal in Q[x]. The same map gives Z[x]/(x)≅Z, a domain but not a field, so (x) is prime but not maximal in Z[x]; indeed (x)⊊(2,x). What changed is the coefficient ring: the quotient is the coefficient ring itself.
3. Decide whether x3+2x+1 is irreducible over Q and over F3.
Solution
Over Q: the rational root test leaves ±1, giving values 4 and −2; no root, degree 3, so irreducible. Over F3: f(0)=1, f(1)=4≡1, f(2)=13≡1; no root, so irreducible, and F3[x]/(x3+2x+1) is a field with 27 elements.
4. Use Eisenstein's criterion to show x4+10x+5 is irreducible over Q. Why does "it has no rational root" not suffice on its own?
Solution
With p=5: 5∤1 (leading coefficient), 5 divides 0,0,10,5, and 25∤5. So it is irreducible. Absence of roots only rules out linear factors; a quartic could still split into two quadratics, as x4+4 does.
5. In F4=F2[x]/(x2+x+1), compute α3, (α+1)2 and α−1.
Solution
α3=α⋅α2=α(α+1)=α2+α=1. (α+1)2=α2+1=α (the cross term 2α is 0). Since α(α+1)=1,

of roots only rules out linear factors; a quartic could still split into two quadratics, as x4+4 does.
5. In F4=F2[x]/(x2+x+1), compute α3, (α+1)2 and α−1.
Solution
α3=α⋅α2=α(α+1)=α2+α=1. (α+1)2=α2+1=α (the cross term 2α is 0). Since α(α+1)=1, α−1=α+1.
6. Show that 3 is irreducible but not prime in Z[−5], using 9=(2+−5)(2−−5).
Solution
N(3)=9. A proper factor would have norm 3, and a2+5b2=3 has no integer solution, so 3 is irreducible. Next, (2+−5)(2−−5)=4+5=9, so 3 divides this product. But 3 divides neither factor, since (2±−5)/3∉Z[−5]. So 3 is not prime.
7. Show that Z[i]/(2+i)≅Z/5Z.
Solution
Let ψ:Z→Z[i]/(2+i) be the natural map. It is surjective: i≡−2 modulo (2+i), so a+bi≡a−2b, an integer. Its kernel contains 5=(2+i)(2−i). If an integer n lies in (2+i), then n=(2+i)γ and n2=N(n)=5N(γ), so 5∣n2 and 5∣n. So the kernel is 5Z, and the First Isomorphism Theorem gives Z/5Z≅Z[i]/(2+i).

Post 05 turns the construction of Chapter 6 into a theory. If p is irreducible over F, the field F[x]/(p) contains a root of p, so it is an extension of F of degree deg⁡p. Degrees multiply in towers, which already settles the Greek problems of doubling the cube and trisecting an angle. Adding all the roots of a polynomial gives its splitting field, and the automorphisms of that field form its Galois group. The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory matches subfields with subgroups, and it explains why there is no formula in radicals for the roots of a general quintic.
